source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Only the physician may report the condition, so nursing and infection-prevention personnel should not participate in notification processes.","B":"Medical-record documentation alone satisfies all reporting duties because public-health notification is optional for reportable conditions.","C":"Reporting is required only when a national outbreak has already been declared, not when an individual state requires notification.","D":"The condition must be reported to the appropriate public-health authority as required by applicable state or local law and procedure."}}
source_row.rationale: Certain diagnoses are classified as "reportable diseases" under state law, requiring notification to the appropriate public health authority (in addition to routine medical record documentation), supporting broader disease surveillance, outbreak identification, and public health response efforts — nurses often play a role in recognizing and facilitating this reporting process, depending on facility protocols.
source_row.source_detail: CDC NNDSS reporting overview: state/local laws and regulations require reporting to public health authorities and requirements vary by jurisdiction; jurisdictions voluntarily notify CDC. Current CDC NNDSS page reviewed 2026-08-15. Reviewed 2026-08-15.
source_row.source_name: CDC / State Health Departments — Reportable Disease Notification Requirements
source_row.stem: A nurse identifies a client with a diagnosis classified as a "reportable disease" in their state, and a colleague assumes this responsibility falls solely to the physician with no expected role for nursing or infection prevention staff. The nurse should instead understand that:
